newsitem.title: FRANCE: French co-ops say EU must rethink grain mkt policy.
newsitem.headline: French co-ops say EU must rethink grain mkt policy.

text.p: The European Union must rethink the organisation of its grain markets or lose export markets to more competitive suppliers, the French grain cooperatives federation FFCAT said on Wednesday.
"If the European Union wants to maintain its position (as a key exporter), it must adapt," FFCAT deputy director general Christian Duval told a news conference.
Faced with record crops at home and tough competition on world markets, EU producers need less restrictive rules to operate, FFCAT officials said.
One key focus should be the new farm bill put forward by rival United States, which they described as a "machine to conquer markets."
They explained that the new bill encouraged U.S. farmers to operate with tight stocks in order to rapidly seize opportunities on export markets.
But while the United States is grabbing market shares, the EU is still trying to manage its own markets using farm land set-asides to regulate stocks, they said.
"We are not saying that operating with tight stocks is good. It can even be dangerous. But if others do it, Europe must follow," Duval said.
The EU expanded in 1992 its farm land set-aside schemes to deal with what then a huge grain surplus.
But in the face of tight supplies and soaring prices the EU agreed in July to halve to five percent the amount of land farmers must keep idle in 1997.

The EU even slapped wheat and barley exports with a tax last year when supplies were low and prices high. But now faced with record crops and strong competition from other suppliers it has restored its grain export subsidies.
But the EU, torn between supplying world markets and rebuilding stocks while also keeping domestic prices under control, has closely monitored the pace of its exports.
Farmers believe the EU must step up its grain exports or it will lose its role as a key exporter.
FFCAT officials also said that EU wheat prices were bound to slip further in order to be competitive with other origins.
They even suggested that producers were not opposed to lower prices for wheat used by the EU animal feed industry.
But faced with the prospect of lower wheat prices they strongly oppose recent proposals to limit aid to the grain sector.
Producers particularly fear recent plans to use part of the aid paid by the EU to grain producers to help cattle producers hit by the scare over the mad cow disease.
"We are saying how can we be competitive on world markets and at the same time help other sectors ?" Duval said. REUTER
